first_check.duty: Real and in force. Visitor Levy (Scotland) Act 2024, s.26: a return within 30 days of each period end, quarterly by default, with one assessment per premises. Penalties are in ss.47-50 and set by each council; further penalties can apply at 3, 6 and 12 months. Edinburgh's penalty framework (marked partly 'recommended, not implemented') gives a first penalty of 1% of rateable value (indicative £81 to £9,870) for non-residential premises and 10% of annual council tax for residential ones. The claimed 'GBP 100 plus 5%' penalty was not confirmed. Edinburgh: 5% of the accommodation charge for the first 5 nights, stays from 24 Jul 2026, bookings paid on or after 1 Oct 2025, 2% reimbursed to providers, records may be inspected. Glasgow: 5% from 25 Jan 2027. Aberdeen has approved 7% (start date not found). Stirling's earliest start is June 2027 and its final decision was not confirmed. Highland has paused its scheme.
first_check.market: Edinburgh had 3,209 short-term let licences in operation at 31 Dec 2025, and 32,317 across Scotland (Scottish Government statistics). Add Edinburgh B&Bs, guest houses and hotels; no count found. No published figure for providers registered on visitorlevy.scot was found. Glasgow joins in Jan 2027 and Aberdeen later, so roughly 4,000 to 6,000 liable small providers is plausible in the near term (an estimate).

first_check.duty: The duty is real, federal and in force. Under § 49 Abs. 4 PBefG, a Mietwagen may only carry out orders that arrive at the firm's base. The firm must record each incoming order in a book or electronically and keep the record for 1 year. After each trip the car must return to the base straight away unless it already has a follow-on order. The current text on gesetze-im-internet.de still contains the return duty. On 2026-06-03 the BGH (I ZR 123/25) upheld the return duty as constitutional and held that breaching it is unfair competition. Enforcement is active. In VG Ansbach AN 10 S 26.536 (16.07.2026), the authority demanded the order register on USB plus machine-readable platform trip data with return times and follow-on order IDs. It counted 67 breaches in 210 trips and revoked permits for 16 cars without a prior warning, and the court upheld this. VGH München 11 ZB 20.2076 upheld a sanction for a badly kept order book. Separately, under § 146a AO, KassenSichV and the BMF letter of 11.03.2024, taximeters and Wegstreckenzähler need a TSE from 2026-01-01. Breaches can be fined up to EUR 25,000 (Härting). The device must also be reported to the Finanzamt via ELSTER within 1 month. One summary says older Wegstreckenzähler with a digital interface may be connected to a TSE until 31.12.2026. Härting and the Berlin LABO page give 1.1.2026 as the hard date. I could not resolve this because the MV Merkblatt PDF was unreadable.
first_check.market: I found no current national count. The DTMV figure via Statista is just over 53,000 taxis in Germany in 2016. The federal survey every four years (last cited for 31.12.2016) and Brandenburg's answer (data held only by districts) give no Mietwagen firm count. Mietwagen permits have no cap, and the Uber/Bolt-driven fleet segment is large in big cities. I estimate roughly 20,000 to 30,000 taxi and Mietwagen firms in total, mostly with 1 to 5 vehicles. This is unverified.
first_check.competitor: The TSE part is crowded: taximeter and Wegstreckenzähler hardware vendors, fiskaly cloud TSE through FMS (per the claim), and Hale. It should be left out of scope. For the order book, the FREENOW AGB require Mietwagen firms to record and forward orders through FREENOW's Fleet Partner Dashboard, so platforms already partly capture order intake. Uber's supplier portal manages the fleet, drivers and revenue. I found no evidence that it produces a § 49 order book. FahrerApp (meinfahrer.app) is Mietwagen-specific telematics with shift recording and seat-occupancy sensors. Its listing does not mention the order book, return-duty proof or TSE. SuE-TaMi Dispo, SOLU Driver and Taxi.de are dispatch tools. Fleetster, Vimcar and R-DRIVE are general electronic logbooks. I found no product that merges platform orders, GPS returns and follow-on order IDs into a register the licensing authority can audit and that flags return-duty breaches. The VG Ansbach case shows authorities now ask for exactly that data.
first_check.reason: The pain is real and rising. The BGH upheld the return duty in June 2026, and VG Ansbach shows permits revoked for a missing or incomplete machine-readable order register. Owner-operators face daily record-keeping. The weak points: the TSE part is solved by hardware vendors. Platforms (FREENOW dashboard, Uber portal) already hold most order data, so a tool would be an aggregation and audit layer. Some heavy Mietwagen users break the return duty on purpose and won't buy proof tools. Political proposals to abolish the return duty add regulatory risk. Buyers are fragmented, price-sensitive and reached through taxi associations or IHK. An MVP needs platform data imports and GPS, so it is not trivial. It is a niche gap worth testing but carries risk.

challenge_check.killer: None found. Partial overlap: Uber's supplier portal and FREENOW's Fleet Partner Dashboard record platform orders, and taximeter and Wegstreckenzähler vendors cover the TSE part. Not checked: whether platform exports satisfy authorities.
challenge_check.reason: Nothing I found kills the claim. § 49(4) PBefG has allowed electronic and app-based order logs since 2021, and the July 2026 amendment did not change § 49. The BGH upheld the return duty on 3 June 2026 (I ZR 123/25). VGH München 11 CS 26.1088 (7 August 2026) upheld revocation of 8 permits after the authority demanded the order book plus app order data on USB and ran a time-series analysis that found 50 return-duty breaches in 175 trips. I found no vendor selling an order book that checks the return duty. Uber's supplier portal and FREENOW's dashboard capture orders but do not check return compliance. The score stays low because many Uber and Bolt fleet owners avoid the duty on purpose, enforcement depends on the authority and is mostly triggered by suspicion, and reform lobbying continues. The TSE part is already crowded.

first_check.duty: Animal Welfare Act (動物愛護管理法) as amended, in force since 2020-06-01. Businesses registered for sale, rental, exhibition or 譲受飼養 (動物販売業者等) must: (a) keep a ledger for 5 years, per animal for dogs and cats and per breed for other mammals, birds and reptiles. first_check.duty: The duty is real and in force. BSP Circular No. 1206 (23 Dec 2024, Monetary Board Res. 1362) removed MORNBFI Secs 901-N and 902-N and replaced them with the M-Regulations. These cover remittance transfer companies, money changers and FX dealers. A second circular, reported as No. 1222 (MB approval 14 Aug 2025), amends the reporting rules in Secs 151-M to 154-M. Secondary summaries say it sets reporting standards, monetary and non-monetary sanctions, and audited financial statement deadlines. I could not open its full text (HTTP 429). Separately, the AML law (RA 9160, as amended by RA 11211) requires: (1) registration with the AMLC on portal.amlc.gov.ph; (2) covered transaction reports for cash over PHP 500,000 in one banking day, due within 5 working days; (3) suspicious transaction reports with no threshold, due the next working day after suspicion arises, filed through GoTRACS. The CTR and STR terms come from secondary sources only, not checked against AMLC text. Enforcement is real: MB cancelled Prince Rockwell, Kings Hopewell and World Reliance for persistent AMLA violations (CL-2025-028), barred 4 unregistered operators (CL-2025-021), and cancelled sole proprietorships (Edzen, World Wide Money Changer). Not verified: exact BSP report forms, how often they are due, and penalty amounts per day of delay.
first_check.market: The claim cites 7,357 registered MSBs at end-2023 (secondary source). Verihubs cites BSP data of about 5,300 head offices, 12,700 branches and 6,700 pawnshops holding MSB licences, but its totals do not add up. Likely buyers are a few thousand single-office changers and remittance agents. I did not find an official 2024 or 2025 count.
first_check.competitor: No product built for small Philippine money changers was found. Tookitaki sells enterprise AML (screening, monitoring, CTR/STR filing). Verihubs sells eKYC, watchlist screening and OCR APIs aimed at agent networks. Foreign bureau-de-change software exists, such as FXPlus, Money Exchanger Plus and CurrencyXchanger on Capterra, but none shows BSP or AMLC reporting. CTR and STR filing goes through the free AMLC portal (GoTRACS), so a product's value would be logging transactions, KYC records, the AML programme document and preparing the files, not the filing itself. Not checked: Philippine POS vendors for forex counters, and whether 247 RemitPlus is still sold.
first_check.reason: The duty is mandatory and enforced: BSP cancels registrations over AML lapses every year, and the M-Regulations were tightened in 2024-25. I found no affordable tool for small money changers. Several things hold the score down. Small changers rarely handle single cash deals over PHP 500k, so routine CTR filing is light. Filing is done on the free AMLC portal. Many operators are cash-only family businesses that are hard to reach and will pay little. Some BSP reporting forms may already be simple templates. A records, KYC and AML-programme pack plus a checklist of BSP reports is a workable MVP. It could be sold through the money changer associations, but the market is only a few thousand firms and willingness to pay is uncertain.

challenge_check.killer: None found. Partial weakeners: AMLC filing through GoTRACS is free; foreign bureau-de-change POS products (CurrencyXchanger, FXPlus, PSTForex) already do the transaction logging, though without BSP or AMLC output; most of the MSB count is probably remittance sub-agents and pawnshops on their principal's systems (my inference, not confirmed).
challenge_check.reason: I found nothing that kills it. No product built for small Philippine money changers turned up. The tools that exist are enterprise AML (Tookitaki), foreign bureau-de-change POS (CurrencyXchanger, FXPlus, PSTForex, which targets Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Thailand) and Mohur's 247 RemitPlus from 2016, with no sign it is still sold. The market is weaker than it looks. Filing through GoTRACS is free. Few small changers will see cash over PHP 500k in a day, so the work is mostly KYC records and STRs. The 7,357 MSB count includes remittance sub-agents, e-money issuers and pawnshops that use their principal's systems. I could not read the text of Circular 1206.

first_check.duty: Firearms Control Act 60 of 2000 and the Firearms Control Regulations, Regulation 37 (dealer registers). Dealers must keep a Firearms Stock Register, an Ammunition Stock Register, a Firearms Safe Custody Register and a staff register, filled in at each receipt and disposal. Registers may be paper books, with every page signed and stamped by the Designated Firearms Officer (DFO) before use, or computer printouts handed to the DFO within 7 days after each month end for signing and stamping. Records are kept for 10 years at the licensed premises. Ammunition returns are due only when the Registrar directs by written notice. The page index lists a separate weekly-returns regulation (Reg 39), but I did not read its text. Breaches are offences under s120(1). SAPS reported 3,728 compliance inspections of gun dealers and security companies (SAnews, 18 Feb 2026), which led to a dealer arrest and the seizure of 537 firearms. The claim cites s39(6), Regulations 38-40 and the 'SAP 350' form; I did not verify those citations. The register rule I confirmed is Reg 37. Security-company armouries also keep registers, and their staff need monthly Regulation 21 training (from job ads; I did not read the regulation itself).

The firearm-holding subset is probably in the low thousands at most. The 3,728 SAPS inspections give a rough upper bound for dealers plus security firms combined. Overall the market is small: probably about 1,000 to 4,000 businesses (my rough estimate).
first_check.competitor: I found no South African dealer or security-firm register software. CybateSoft (South Africa) does weapon marking and track-and-trace, but its listing does not mention SAPS register formats. The state Firearms Control Management System (FCMS) is still rolling out in phases. Its Release 02 was pushed to the end of January 2026, and a pilot is planned at three Gauteng police stations. I found no go-live date and no dealer portal. Dealers and gunsmiths do sit on a Technical Work Team for FCMS, so a future state dealer interface remains a risk. I did not check for a locally built dealer point-of-sale system with a register module or with in-house spreadsheets, beyond these searches.
first_check.reason: The duty is real and enforced. Regulation 37 of the Firearms Control Regulations requires dealers to keep firearm stock, ammunition stock, safe-custody and staff registers for 10 years. If a dealer keeps them on computer, it must hand printouts to the Designated Firearms Officer within 7 days of each month end for signing and stamping, so the work recurs every month. SAPS reported 3,728 inspections of dealers and security firms in February 2026, and breaches are offences under s120(1). I found no South African software for these registers. Available tools are US ATF/FFL point-of-sale systems or generic armoury systems. Weaknesses: the market is small and could not be counted, buyers are wary of sharing sensitive data, paper books remain legal, and a dealer channel in FCMS could make the product redundant.

The district or city Dinkes issues SLHS after a sanitarian's inspection (IKL) and a lab result no older than 1 month. Validity is 3 years in one source and 2 years in another (unverified). first_check.reason: The duties are real: NIB/OSS, an SLHS from Dinkes, and lab tests at least every 6 months. first_check.duty: Real and in force. Since 1 Jan 2026 the NLMA's (國土管理署) nationwide full-flow regime for construction surplus soil (營建剩餘土石方) applies. Every trip from site to receiving yard needs an electronic manifest (電子聯單) showing the project, route, soil type and volume, and every truck must carry a GPS unit that has passed NLMA type approval. The type-approval procedure is published on nlma.gov.tw. The NLMA gave a GPS transition buffer to the end of February 2026 and opened GPS applications to small trucks. The frequency is every trip. Penalties are not uniform yet: enforcement currently runs through the administrative scheme and local rules, and I did not find a specific national fine. The draft Waste Disposal Act Article 10-1 (MOENV notice of 29 May 2025) would make online reporting and GPS mandatory and let MOI set national rules and penalties. UDN reported on 18 May 2026 that the bill was only in Legislative Yuan committee review. One summary mentions a third reading, but I could not date it or confirm that the soil clause survived. Treat the amendment as pending or unverified.

I could not confirm whether the state system offers an API or data export, so integration risk is high.

But the state e-manifest system is free, and GPS vendors already bundle fleet tracking, so the remaining gap is only the dispatch and ledger layer that ties manifests to fees and costs. Small haulers are fragmented owner-operators who are not very digital and are price-sensitive (GPS units sell for around NT$380). Whether the state system has an API is unknown, which makes the MVP risky. The pending Waste Disposal Act changes may alter the rules again. The UAF fines these sectors heavily: real-estate firms were among the most sanctioned in 2021, mostly for a missing manual or missing training. Gesintel's AMLupdate is aimed at notaries and large firms, not small brokers. I found no broker-specific SME tool. The market is small: about 1,037 brokers and 478 inmobiliarias in 2015. trigger: Res UIF 43/2024 (national): biennial risk self-assessment filed by 30 April, external independent reviewer report within 120 days after, systematic monthly and annual reports, client risk segmentation, suspicious-transaction alert signals. First deadlines 30 Apr 2026 and 31 Aug 2026 have passed; the next cycle and follow-up inspections are ahead.

first_check.duty:
Res UIF 43/2024 is national law and in force since 18 Mar 2024; the official consolidated text is on argentina.gob.ar. It covers matriculated real estate brokers and brokerage firms run by matriculated brokers, when they handle sales or leases of at least 300 SMVM a year. Duties:
- A risk self-assessment (Informe Técnico), updated every 2 years and filed by 30 April. The first was due 30 Apr 2026, so the next is due Apr 2028.
- An external independent reviewer (REI) every 2 years, within 120 days after the self-assessment deadline, for firms with income above 875 SMVM or 50+ activities a year. The first was due 31 Aug 2026.
- An internal audit instead of the REI for legal persons below those thresholds.
- Monthly systematic reports between the 1st and 15th of each month.
- An annual report (RSA) between 2 Jan and 15 Mar.
- A compliance officer, client risk segmentation with simplified, medium or enhanced due diligence, and alert signals.
Penalties: Art. 35 refers to Chapter IV of Law 25.246; I did not check the amounts. I found no 2026 extension for brokers. The 2026 extensions I found were for accountants (REI moved to 1 Mar 2027) and lawyers (Res 90/2026). There is no simplified regime for small firms.
first_check.market: No official count of obligated brokers was found. CUCICBA (Buenos Aires city) had 7,084 registered agencies in 2018 (BAE Negocios). FIRA estimates more than 70,000 agencies nationwide (iProfesional, Feb 2025); this is an industry-body figure and likely includes unregistered agencies. Only matriculated brokers that actually close sales or large leases are obligated, so a plausible range is roughly 10,000 to 25,000 firms (unverified). Risk: in Feb 2025 the government proposed ending mandatory colegiación for brokers; it was not enacted as of that article. If enacted, it could change who counts as an obligated subject.
first_check.competitor: Free state channel: UIF's SRO/SRO+ portal and the SROMasivo application handle the monthly report (RSM) filing for property sales, with a defined form (buyer and seller, PEP status, payment method). The state therefore covers the report submission step, but not the risk matrix, client file and due diligence management, the self-assessment or alert monitoring. Free templates: the FACPCE ITAER guide and matrix, and the property registry's (DNRPI) matrix. Real estate CRMs (Tokko Broker, Xintel) showed no AML or UIF module in my searches. I found no broker-specific AML SaaS, though the search was not exhaustive. The main alternatives are compliance law firms (for example stabogados) and accountants.
first_check.reason: The duty is real and current. The monthly and annual reports are ongoing, and the self-assessment and external review (REI) recur every two years. Nothing dedicated does the core work of the risk matrix, client segmentation, client file and due diligence, and alert monitoring for brokers. However, the UIF's free SROMasivo/SRO already handles the monthly report submission. The heavy deliverables, the self-assessment and REI, are biennial (next due Apr/Aug 2028) and are usually bought from accountants or lawyers. Many small brokers have few qualifying operations and enforcement looks light, so willingness to pay is uncertain. Distribution through the provincial broker colegios is feasible. An MVP covering client risk scoring, the client file and RSM export is simple. Partnering with accountants who do the REI could help.

challenge_check.killer: None found. Partial overlap: UIF's free SRO/SRO+ portal for the monthly report; the free FACPCE ITAER guide and matrix; CONLAFT S.R.L. AML platform, which targets other obligated sectors and doesn't mention brokers. Risk to watch: a draft bill to deregulate broker licensing (May 2026, not confirmed as filed).
challenge_check.reason: I found no product, free tool or rule that does the whole job for brokers under Res UIF 43/2024. The one local AML platform I found, CONLAFT, sells to mutuales, cooperatives and accountants, not brokers. I found no AML module from Tokko or Xintel, and no broker-specific extension of the deadlines. The 2026 extension to March 2027 covers accountants (Res 42/2024), not brokers. The weak points: UIF's free SRO portal already handles the monthly report. The self-assessment is only due every two years, so the next one is likely in 2028. The external review only applies to larger firms. Free templates exist (the FACPCE ITAER guide). Small brokers may not pay much, and enforcement is uneven. A government bill to drop the mandatory broker licence (reported May 2026, status unknown) could blur who is obliged, since the rules cover licensed brokers. Market: COFECI says it has 35,000+ licensed members, but the number of active UIF-registered brokers is unknown.

first_check.duty: Real and in force. INAES Res 1279/2026 was signed on 23-06-2026 and published in the Boletin Oficial No. 35937 on 25-06-2026. It applies to mutuales under the monthly regime of Res 1418/03 art. 17(b) (text ordered by Res 3034/2024). Each month, within 20 business days of month end, they must report compliance with arts. 5, 6, 9 and 10 (Annexes I-V and VII) to INAES and to the local provincial authority. It applies from the July 2026 period, and overdue periods must also be filed through the new system. The resolution itself sets no penalty. Enforcement comes from other rules: Res 1687/2026 gave lending mutuales 30 days to cure missing filings, and Res 878/879/2024 ordered sumarios against thousands of non-compliant entities (secondary sources). Separately, Res 756/2025 requires all co-operatives and mutuales to file a member and authorities roll every year, and quarterly if they are UIF 99/2023 obligated parties (deadline extended by Res 2147/2025). Lending mutuales are UIF obligated parties.
first_check.market: No current national count was found. An older Mercado article cites about 32,000 registered co-operatives and mutuales, but the figure is undated and the register has since been purged; INAES suspended 20,612 co-operatives and 1,847 mutuales in 2019. In 2020 Santa Fe had 850 mutuales, of which 300 offered ayuda economica. The lending-mutual segment that carries the monthly duty is probably around 1,000 to 2,000 nationally, but this is an extrapolation and unverified.
first_check.competitor: The filing itself goes through INAES's own free web system. According to the resolution text, it completely replaces the spreadsheet download and upload flow. It offers manual web entry with validations, autocomplete and partial save, and issues a PDF receipt. No file import or API was found. That means a third-party tool cannot simply generate a file to upload; it would need assisted entry or browser automation, which makes an MVP harder. Mutual management ERPs exist: Grupo Neo Sistemas (NeoConsultores S.A.) sells an integral system for mutuales, with the MutualOnline app. Whether any ERP prepares the INAES annex data was not confirmed. A generic member tool, Gestion Socios, has no INAES features. No vendor was found that specifically offers INAES filing for mutuales.
first_check.reason: The duty is real, monthly and newly changed: from July 2026 the new INAES web system replaces the old spreadsheets and is manual entry only, and overdue periods must be re-entered there. That creates fresh pain for lending mutuales. However, the filing channel is free, the reachable segment is small (probably low thousands of lending mutuales), and the mid-size ones likely already run mutual ERPs such as Neo Sistemas, which may add INAES support. Because there is no import path, a third-party tool would depend on browser automation, which is brittle. Many entities have volunteer boards, so willingness to pay is doubtful. Distribution through accountants and provincial federations is plausible. The yearly or quarterly member roll adds some recurring value.

challenge_check.killer: None found. The partial threats are INAES's own free web transmission system (Res 1279/2026), accountants who already serve mutuales, and the chance that mutual ERPs such as Grupo Neo Sistemas add the INAES annexes.
challenge_check.reason: Nothing kills it. Spanish searches found no vendor that files the INAES ayuda economica return or the nomina for mutuales. The only mutual ERP found was Grupo Neo Sistemas (MutualOnline app), and no INAES export was confirmed for it. INAES Res 1567/2026 (published 3 Aug 2026) adds another recurring duty on the same web system: an AML module with annual sworn statements, a quarterly statistical ROS report and an initial filing within 90 days. That widens the bundle. The weaknesses stay: filing goes through INAES's free web entry, with no import or API found. Accountants and the Consejo Profesional advisory desk already serve these entities. The number of active lending mutuales was not found. The buyers are volunteer boards, and the work is mostly data entry, not a tool gap.

first_check.duty: UIF Res. 55/2024 (in force since 26/03/2024), under Ley 25.246 art. 20 inc. 16. Clients are defined at 6 or more SMVM. The monthly RSM covers operations over 20 SMVM and is filed between days 1 and 15; a "sin movimientos" report is required in months with nothing to report. The annual RSA is filed between 2 Jan and 15 Mar. The ITAER risk self-assessment and the risk tolerance declaration are due every two years by 30 April (first deadline 30/04/2026, covering 2024 and 2025). Legal persons need a compliance officer and an internal audit. An independent external review is required above 180 SMVM a year (first report due by 31/10/2026). Sanctions follow Ley 25.246 Ch. IV. Res. 54/2024 covers art, antiques and numismatics, not jewellery. Registration in SRO+ was fully digitalised by Res. 37/2026. I could not open the 2025 Boletín Oficial notice (aviso 305168, 503 error), so it is not_reached.
first_check.market: Unverified. I found no UIF statistic on how many inc. 16 entities are registered, and the UIF 2024 management summary PDF could not be parsed. The scope is broad (mining, gold buyers, refiners, manufacturers, artisans, retailers), but how many are actually registered and above the thresholds is unknown, and enforcement against small informal gold buyers is likely weak.
first_check.competitor: Reports are filed on UIF's free SRO+ portal, which handles submission but not record-keeping, risk scoring or the self-assessment. Three Spanish-language searches for Argentine AML software (jewellers, DNFBPs, RSM/legajo) found no jeweller-specific product. The only jeweller-specific AML tool that came up, kyc-systems.com, is Mexican (LFPIORPI). Accountants and AML consultants offer generic services, and the professional councils (consejo.org.ar, FACPCE) publish self-assessment guides for their own members. Regional or generic AML vendors were not checked exhaustively.
first_check.reason: The duty is real and in force. UIF Res. 55/2024 (BO 26/03/2024, which replaced Res. 28/2011) covers the whole jewellery and precious-metal chain down to retailers and artisans. It requires a monthly RSM report (days 1-15, operations over 20 SMVM, or a "sin movimientos" filing when there are none), an annual RSA (2 Jan-15 Mar) and a two-yearly risk self-assessment due by 30 April (first one in 2026). It also requires a compliance officer and an internal audit, plus an external review above 180 SMVM a year. Penalties follow Ley 25.246 Ch. IV. Filing itself goes through UIF's free SRO+ portal. I found no jeweller-specific Argentine AML software. Downsides: I found no figure for how many firms are in scope, many small jewellers are informal, willingness to pay is likely low, and accountants already sell this as a service.

challenge_check.killer: None found. There is no Argentine jeweller-specific AML product, no free UIF tool beyond the filing portal, and no exemption for small firms.
challenge_check.reason: The duty is real and recurring. Res. 55/2024 covers the whole jewellery and precious-metal chain with no size exemption. It requires a monthly RSM for operations above 20 SMVM, an annual RSA, a compliance officer, an annual manual review, annual training records, and a two-yearly self-assessment (first due 30 Apr 2026). Firms above 180 SMVM a year also need an external review (first due 31 Oct 2026); smaller legal persons need an internal audit. Five searches found no Argentine AML software for these firms, only law and consulting firms. Risks: the market size is unknown, past enforcement was weak (2014: fines of AR$221.7M imposed, about AR$250k collected), and thresholds may be revised. Accountants pressed UIF in 2026 for extensions and new thresholds, and UIF already moved accountants' external review to March 2027.

first_check.duty: Ley 27693 makes casinos and slot-machine operators reporting entities. Res. SBS 01015-2026 (dated 6 Apr 2026, published in El Peruano 8 Apr 2026) updates Res. SBS 1695-2016 and also amends the sanctions regulation (Res. SBS 5389-2013). It covers legal entities that run casinos and/or slot machines, and for the first time remote games, remote sports betting and betting rooms. Duties: a risk-based SPLAFT with 13 minimum components; a compliance officer accredited to the UIF (exclusive or part-time, plus an alternate; designation reported within 15 business days); due diligence on clients, workers and suppliers; checks against UN lists and asset freezes; annual staff training; internal and external audit; operations register; suspicious-transaction reports (ROS) filed via ROSEL; an annual compliance-officer report (IAOC) sent to MINCETUR and the UIF. Anonymous betting is eliminated. A new alert-reporting guide via ROSEL (Res. SBS 01219-2026, 24 Apr 2026) also applies to reporting entities. MINCETUR supervises and sanctions. A search summary attributed to press coverage put fines at up to about 8 UIT for the gravest failures; I did not confirm this, and a 2023 PRCP infographic on the general regime gave 7-100 UIT for very serious breaches. Not verified: effective date, adaptation window, and whether there are casino-specific register thresholds (the general rule is USD 10k per operation and USD 50k per month for multiple operations).
first_check.market: MINCETUR's vice-minister (El Peruano, July 2026) cited 19 authorised casinos and 714 registered slot rooms with about 72,500 machines. The number of distinct legal entities is lower because chains own many rooms; the exact count was not found. Remote betting and gaming platforms are newly in scope (MINCETUR has authorised and blocks many; count not verified). Penalty pressure is real: in Jan-Aug 2022 MINCETUR made 1,346 inspections and sanctioned 10 firms for not filing the annual compliance-officer report.
first_check.competitor: I found no commercial SPLAFT software aimed at Peruvian gaming in three Spanish searches (gaming-specific, consultancy/outsourced compliance officer, general PLAFT software for Peru). State tools: SUCTR (online monitoring of all ~72.5k machines for MINCETUR/SUNAT, not AML), ROSEL and the PLAFT portal (filing channels only), and SBS list-check pages. Law firms such as PRCP publish SPLAFT guides, which suggests a consulting market exists. Not checked: international and LatAm AML/KYC SaaS, casino-management or player-tracking systems that may include AML modules, and in-house systems at large chains.
first_check.reason: The duty is real. Res. SBS 01015-2026 (dated 6 Apr, published 8 Apr 2026) updates Res. SBS 1695-2016 under Ley 27693. It requires a risk-based SPLAFT with 13 minimum components (compliance officer, due diligence, annual training, audit, operations register, STRs, annual compliance-officer report) and now covers remote and sports betting. MINCETUR supervises and fines; it fined 10 firms in 2022 for missing the annual report. About 714 registered slot rooms plus 19 casinos (July 2026). Searches found no Peru-specific gaming SPLAFT software, but law firms and consultants serve the sector. LatAm AML tools and casino-management systems were not checked. Many rooms belong to chains, the compliance officer can be part-time, and the adaptation deadline is unverified. The niche is real but small.

challenge_check.killer: None found. Weak points: the regime replaces Res. SBS 1695-2016, which already applied, so incumbents have existing SPLAFT setups and consultants. The market is about 325 licensed firms (undated MINCETUR presentation, apparently from 2023). Enforcement is modest: 10 firms fined in 2022 for not filing the compliance-officer report.
challenge_check.reason: I found no killer. No local or international SPLAFT software for Peruvian gaming came up, and the state tools (ROSEL, SISDEL, SUCTR) are only filing or machine-monitoring channels. Three things keep the score low. First, the duty isn't new: Res. SBS 01015-2026 replaces Res. 1695-2016, so slot-room operators already have compliance officers and SPLAFT manuals, and many likely use outside consultants such as PRCP. Second, the market is small: an undated MINCETUR presentation to Congress, apparently from 2023, counts about 325 licensed firms running 711 rooms. Online operators are new to the regime but probably use international KYC tools. Third, enforcement is light: 10 firms were fined in 2022 for missing the annual compliance-officer report. Still not checked: the adaptation deadline, any small-firm regime, and RO thresholds. Two key sources returned 403.

first_check.duty: Section 61 of the Co-operative Societies Act 1993 (Act 502), restated in SKM guideline GP26 of 1 Sep 2024: accounts must be audited at least once each financial year by an SKM-approved auditor. Koperasi that run no business, hold no AGM and have no audit for more than 3 years face cancellation (SKM Negeri Sembilan director, BH Apr 2026). first_check.duty: Ley 23 of 2015 and DE 35/2022, plus Acuerdo JD-02-2022 for lawyers and accountants: client due diligence, beneficial-owner identification, risk-based matrix, prevention manual, UAF liaison and reports, and an annual update of high-risk client files (per the KPMG guide). Ley 124/2020 requires SSNF registration, with a $5,000 fine for resident agents who don't register. Res. S-022-2025 of 21 Mar 2025, published in Gaceta Oficial 30248 on 1 Apr 2025, requires the self-assessment questionnaires. The questionnaire's periodicity and deadline could not be confirmed: the PDF was too large to fetch. Sanctions are reported at USD 5,000 to 5 million (Chambers).
first_check.market: About 12,000 sujetos obligados no financieros were registered with the SSNF over 2020-2024, more than 60% of them lawyers (La Estrella, 24 Mar 2025). A separate count of 7,500 resident agents is cited in the same article. Earlier SSNF data show 664 law firms and 2,271 individual lawyers registered (as of 2022).
first_check.competitor: No dedicated Panamanian product for SONF compliance (SSNF registration, the questionnaire, the risk matrix and UAF reporting) was found in Spanish or English searches. The free SSNF online app (Res. S-010-2021) handles registration and probably the questionnaire submission; that is unconfirmed. Generic AML/KYC screening vendors pitch Panama (Didit's AML screening API, Sanction Scanner). Consultants offer guidance, for example KPMG's SONF obligations guide. Outsourced compliance-officer services were not checked (not_reached).
first_check.reason: The duty is real and current. Ley 23/2015, Ley 124/2020 (the SSNF law, art. 43 amended by Ley 254/2021), DE 35/2022 and Acuerdo JD-02-2022 put KYC, a risk matrix, a prevention manual and UAF reporting on lawyers and accountants. Res. S-022-2025 (Gaceta 30248, 1 Apr 2025) adds risk self-assessment questionnaires. About 12,000 SONF are registered, over 60% of them lawyers. No Panama-specific SONF compliance software turned up; I found only generic KYC/screening APIs (Didit, Sanction Scanner) and Big-4 guides. The catch is that registration and the questionnaire are filed free through the SSNF online app. The paid value would be ongoing due diligence and the risk matrix, which is closer to generic KYC tooling. The questionnaire frequency is unverified. Small firms are price-sensitive, and some lawyers are giving up resident-agent work instead of complying.

challenge_check.killer: No killer. AgileCheck Express is a partial competitor (screening and risk matrix only). Not verified: the scope of the free SSNF app and the questionnaire deadlines.
challenge_check.reason: Nothing I found does the whole job. AgileCheck Express is the closest partial competitor: its Software Advice/GetApp listings say it covers Panama's SSNF and sells to law firms, accountants and realtors on per-use credits, with sanctions/PEP screening and a weighted risk matrix. But the vendor's own site is aimed at Venezuela and does not mention the SSNF questionnaire, registration or UAF reports. Didit and Shufti only do screening. The duty is getting stricter: Res. S-008-2026 requires enhanced due diligence on PEPs, and a sworn statement under JD-02-2022 was due 1 Dec 2025. The market may be smaller than claimed, since lawyers are dropping the resident-agent role because SSNF and UAF compliance costs more than it earns. The free SSNF app's scope and the questionnaire deadlines are still unverified.
